verdict.text:
Track 1 is measurable here, unlike runs with empty gold labels: there are 31 genuinely-missing slots across the 30 requirements, so the numbers mean something — but they are unevenly distributed, and only the condition slot (21 missing cases) carries enough weight to support a claim. Few-shot flagged 8 of those 21, silently inventing a condition in the other 13. Crucially, when it did flag, it was never wrong: precision 1.0 on condition, and 1.0 at the run-level completeness verdict. So the failure mode is not spurious incompleteness warnings, it is under-reporting. The model treats an unconditioned feature request as if a triggering event were obvious and manufactures one. 801-Signal is the clean illustration: all three humans wrote `<MISSING_CONDITION>` and framed the requirement as "the App must allow the user to mute…", while the LLM asserted "when the user activates the 'Mute' option" — a UI interaction the source text never specifies. 6031, 757, 5775, 828 and 7310 follow the identical pattern.

The action slot is the more worrying cell, even though its support is only 5: flag rate 0.0, five for five silently filled. 496-Signal shows why. The request is a bare title ("Ability to change maximum size of MMS") plus a thank-you note; two of three humans refused to state an action at all, and the LLM produced a fully-formed requirement. 4333-Signal is the extreme case — every slot gold-missing, every slot filled, a URL-only description turned into a confident conditional requirement. Five cases cannot establish a rate, but this is precisely the fabrication the study is designed to catch, and it deserves a targeted follow-up with more sparse-description requirements rather than a broader random sample. Scope (n=1) and actor/modalVerb (n=2 each) are uninterpretable; ignore those f1 values.

Similarity sits slightly above the human ceiling on all three measures — seq_ratio 0.617 vs 0.576, cosine 0.727 vs 0.663, jaccard 0.491 vs 0.473. With standard deviations near 0.27–0.35 over ~88 pairs these gaps are not meaningful separately, but the consistent direction supports the honest reading: the LLM's phrasing is as close to any given human as the humans are to each other. Conversion form is not the bottleneck; the missing-slot judgment is. Note the ceiling itself is low, driven by annotators disagreeing about whether to write a requirement at all (83-Signal: two refuse, one writes one) — the same disagreement Track 1 measures.

Paska's 83% pass is dominated by the two cases where the LLM correctly declined to fill slots: 83-Signal and 592-Signal both trip "Not requirement," which is arguably the detector penalising the right behaviour rather than finding a defect. Of the genuine smells, 828-Signal (condition after the response, plus passive voice) and 7310-Signal (imprecise verb) are minor surface issues. 6457-Signal's non-atomic flag is notable given non-atomic requirements were excluded upstream — worth checking whether the LLM introduced a second action during conversion.

Next step: hold the strategy fixed and enlarge the condition-missing and action-missing strata specifically, and decide whether Paska should exempt legitimately-incomplete outputs before pass_rate is compared across strategies.
